title: The Incomplete Realism — Eddie Would Go
units: Essay · 10 min read
The Incomplete Realism
When foreign policy stops halfway between idealism and pragmatism, the result is a strategy that satisfies no one.
15 March 2026 · Essay
«The law of the plains is the law of the strongest.»
— Rómulo Gallegos, Doña Bárbara (1929)

The detention of Nicolás Maduro has prompted a wave of analysis criticising the United States for lacking a clear plan for Venezuela's transition. The argument runs that while the military operation was a success, the political component remains opaque. That reading is a mistake.

What can be observed from Washington is not confusion but the application of a hard, pragmatic realism, willing to accept a scenario far from the democratic ideal in exchange for immediate, low-cost geopolitical results. The scenario now emerging carries a high price: a government headed by Delcy Rodríguez, with much of the Chavista structure still holding key positions of power — her brother Jorge Rodríguez at the head of the Legislative Assembly, Defence Minister Vladimir Padrino López still in post, and Diosdado Cabello as Interior Minister.

At that cost, what is obtained is a controlled transition. Washington grasped one fundamental fact with precision: María Corina Machado, despite her courage and the majority support of a section of the Venezuelan people, has not managed to fracture the core of real power — the repressive apparatus.

Neither after the disputed elections nor during the mass demonstrations was there any public rupture within the Armed Forces or the Bolivarian National Guard. Placing Machado in power without that internal coercive capacity would be to plunge the country into anomic chaos, into a quasi-civil war in which her victory is by no means guaranteed, especially if the regime turns to Cuban or Russian support for repression.

Faced with this dilemma, the options for an opposition-led transition are unworkable. A direct US military intervention would carry a prohibitive political and economic cost, contrary to the America First doctrine and to the new Republican isolationism. An international or Latin American force is a chimera, blocked by the Chinese and Russian veto on the Security Council and by the lack of will among regional powers such as Brazil, Colombia or Mexico.

The operation as executed therefore follows a logic of realpolitik: decapitate the supreme leader and negotiate with the regime's heirs, who, controlling the means of coercion, "hold the whip hand". The show of force exposed the obsolescence of Venezuela's defences, the penetration of its intelligence services and the vulnerability of Chavismo. Now the pressure shifts to the regime to settle its internal disputes — between Cabello, the Rodríguez siblings and Cuban influence — and reach an accommodation with Washington.

Such a pact would imply, at a minimum, distancing from Cuba and Nicaragua, the severing of close ties with China and Russia, and the opening of strategic sectors of the Venezuelan economy to American capital.

This narrative of an effective realism, however, contains critical omissions and assumes a linearity that Venezuelan reality defies. Its principal flaw is the fallacy of total control. It assumes that Maduro can be removed and a transitional government installed while the Chavista structure remains intact and cohesive. This view underestimates the deep fragmentation of real power in Venezuela. According to analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the InSight Crime foundation, the Armed Forces are not a monolithic bloc but a network of "cartels of the generals" controlling the trafficking of drugs, gold and petrol across different regions.

Their loyalty to a new central government will depend on the preservation of their illicit businesses, not on ideological allegiance. A power struggle between these factions could result in the violent fragmentation of the territory rather than an orderly transition. The capacity of Russia and China to destabilise is also underestimated. Having lost an ally, their objective could well be to sabotage a US-sponsored transition. Russia, with military technical personnel and cyber capabilities in the country, could back loyal factions to create a prolonged conflict, turning Venezuela into a new point of asymmetric tension that consumes American resources and attention.

The analysis also overlooks the humanitarian and migratory factor as a source of regional pressure. Close to 8 million Venezuelans have fled, causing the collapse of services in neighbouring countries. Any "stable agreement" that does not rapidly reverse this crisis will be a failure in the eyes of Latin American governments, eroding whatever benefit the operation is perceived to have delivered. Stability requires a flow of food and medicine, not just oil investment.

There is a third plausible scenario: the decapitation of the regime could precipitate an internal struggle resulting in multiple zones of control — a nominal government in Caracas, regions under autonomous military command (such as Guayana) and areas dominated by Colombian-Venezuelan guerrillas. This scenario would force a regional response. While Brazil under Lula rejects intervention, a shared security crisis in the Amazon could push the Brazilian Army — with its historic doctrine of protecting the frontier — towards unilateral containment actions, creating a new focus of continental tension. This scenario is unlikely.

The operation can be read as a "success" within a transactional worldview: eliminate a nemesis, demonstrate strength and open up commercial opportunities. Success will be measured by Washington's ability to deliver a "stable, business-friendly Venezuela" — and all the more so if it is democratic; failure will be a "failed state administered by military oligarchs", mired in perpetual humanitarian crisis. The greatest risk is not military failure but political failure. A transition that entrenches figures sanctioned for corruption and human rights violations, while ignoring the National Assembly elected in 2015 and the leaders of the civilian opposition, would destroy the democratic legitimacy of the process.

That would alienate key allies in the European Union and Latin America, leaving the United States alone, administering an informal protectorate over a fractured country and bearing the full burden of its reconstruction without international consensus. This consequence directly contradicts the America First doctrine of avoiding onerous commitments.

The lesson of past interventions is clear: a tyrant can be toppled with relative ease, but peace and stability are built only on broad consensus and economic growth. In ignoring this premise, Washington's strategy risks failing to resolve the Venezuelan problem at all; it merely changes its shape, running the risk of creating a crisis that is deeper, costlier and more destabilising for the entire region. Time will tell whether this calculation, made in the coldness of realism, proves a strategic success or a historic error of the first order — and whether Rómulo Gallegos's description still applies to the Venezuela of the twenty-first century.
